themes.definition: The people and mix of expertise a public body is told to assemble, or to have access to, in order to build, buy, test and run an AI tool.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Playbook (UK174) goes furthest: at the outset of a project 'you need to form a service team', the 'minimum viable AI team must be able to' identify user needs, 'design, build, test and iterate AI products' and ensure responsible use, and the team 'should include or be able to collaborate with' business experts, data scientists, software engineers, user researchers and legal, commercial, security, ethics and data-privacy colleagues. Other documents name similar mixes for narrower purposes: interdisciplinary teams with legal, technical and domain expertise as an expected audit control (UK268); a multidisciplinary team, with named roles from data architect to commercial manager, to support procurement and to evaluate tenders (UK136); information-governance teams brought in early (UK099); and, for records-management uses, a knowledge and information management (KIM) team supported by data scientists, technical specialists, the solution provider and senior management, with the warning that a data-science environment needs 'a trained data scientist, data engineer or data analyst' (AI_Insights). Ofgem (UK010) frames the same need as competence: roles assigned to people with appropriate knowledge, access to 'the necessary competence', and those responsible for AI risk management suitably experienced. UK266 is one of the few places where testing competence is named as a staff need, listing 'model assurance' among the specialist capabilities an organisation 'will need'; UK099 alone ties team make-up to fairness (a diverse team, and where that is not possible, note the gaps and engage stakeholders). Tools for building teams are pointed to (the Digital and Data Profession Capability Framework, the Service Manual), but no document supplies staff: all of this is required of the public body itself.
themes.holders: 'You' / the organisation and its project or service team (UK174, UK099, UK136); the organisation (UK268, UK266); 'stakeholders' in the energy sector and 'those responsible for AI risk management and treatment' (UK010); KIM teams, senior leaders and senior management (AI_Insights); a lead assigned to complete ATRS records (UK086).
themes.binding: Non-statutory guidance throughout. UK174 uses 'must' and 'need to' for forming the team and its minimum capabilities and 'should' for its composition; UK136, UK099 and UK010 use 'should', 'seek to', 'recommend' and 'good practice'; AI_Insights states conditions ('you will need' a data scientist if a data-science environment is chosen). No consequence for not meeting any of these is stated.
themes.checks: Partly. The team is meant to 'design, build, test and iterate AI products' (UK174); user researchers are brought in so that evaluation is designed in (UK174); UK266 names model assurance capability; UK136 uses the multidisciplinary team to evaluate tenders. Trigger: outset of the project (UK174) or procurement (UK136). Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the team. What happens with the result: not stated.

themes.theme: In-house capability, outsourcing and knowledge transfer
themes.definition: Whether the skills to run and check an AI tool sit inside the public body or are bought in from contractors, consultants and suppliers, and how knowledge is kept when outsiders or key people leave.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 accepts a mixed model 'Considering the current shortage of AI talent' (new hires, contractors or third parties, internal upskilling), asks for a sourcing and partnership strategy defining which capabilities are built in-house and which are sought from partners, and asks teams to plan knowledge transfer and training 'to ensure the model’s sustainable management'. UK136 (procurement) makes knowledge transfer and training part of the requirement placed on the supplier, asks buyers to evaluate the supplier's knowledge-transfer plan, and, if internal teams cannot run the tool alone, to establish in-house capacity by hiring and retaining staff or through further maintenance contracts. UK268 treats dependence on consultants as an audit risk: internal staff should have acquired the knowledge of the roles once consultants leave, and succession and handover arrangements are 'critical'. UK266 pushes hardest against outsourcing: audit and risk assurance committees are to ask whether there is adequate in-house capability 'rather than treating AI as a purely technical or outsourced issue', and whether risks to entry-level learning and long-term capability are managed. UK071 adds that staff who act as 'safety backstops (e.g. validating AI outputs)' may lose skills, and organisations should assess that risk. UK082 recommends hiring external AI talent with pay benchmarked to at least 75% of the private-sector rate, and UK010 suggests proofs of concept and partnerships to build capability. [inference] UK174's openness to contractors and UK266's warning against outsourcing are a difference of emphasis rather than a direct contradiction.
themes.holders: Departments and project teams ('you', UK174, UK136); the auditee's internal personnel (UK268); the organisation, questioned by audit and risk assurance committees (UK266); organisations (UK071); stakeholders (UK010); government (UK082, as a recommendation).
themes.binding: All advisory: 'consider', 'should', imperatives in guidance, 'critical', and questions for committees. UK082 items are recommendations whose acceptance is not recorded in the document. UK268 names the risk if not met ('Lack of defined processes for transition, succession planning, and handover'); no other consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Two links to checking. (1) UK071: assess the risk of skill loss where staff validate AI outputs or may need to recover manually; trigger: placed in the continuous monitoring module (ongoing); compared against: not stated; metric: not stated; who: organisations; result: not stated. (2) UK136: buyers evaluate the supplier's knowledge-transfer plan at contract implementation; compared against: whether internal teams 'will be able to use the tool appropriately on their own'; metric: not stated; result: if this cannot be guaranteed, hire and retain staff or buy maintenance contracts.

themes.theme: Organisation-wide AI literacy, training plans and workforce planning
themes.definition: Requirements that a public body train its staff in AI generally, set the AI knowledge each role needs, and adjust roles and workforce plans accordingly.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 and UK266 use almost the same sentence: 'You and your team' (UK174) or 'Organisations' (UK266) 'should gain the skills needed to use, design, build and maintain AI solutions'. UK266 adds that a much broader group of staff 'will need basic AI literacy', so organisations must invest in reskilling, update professional standards and job roles, plan for risks to entry-level learning, and have 'credible plans for upskilling staff from basic AI literacy to specialist skills'. Ofgem (UK010) is the most procedural: define a baseline of AI knowledge for all staff 'including ensuring appropriate training and testing of internal knowledge', agree role-specific levels, implement a training and development plan, update knowledge-management policies, and horizon-scan so learning plans stay current. The NAO strategy is the only document that commits its own body to deliver: baseline AI training for all staff 'covering responsible use, risks and professional judgement', specialist expertise and updated role expectations. AI_Insights adds training in developer onboarding and budgets for ongoing training; UK099 and UK206 state the need briefly. Who pays, how much time is allowed and what standard training must meet are not stated (UK174's five-day entitlement is in the next theme).
themes.holders: 'You and your team' (UK174); organisations (UK266, UK206); teams (UK099); 'stakeholders' (UK010); the NAO for its own staff (NAO_AI_Strategy); the organisation or team onboarding developers, and leadership as nearest named actor for training budgets (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: Non-statutory: 'should', 'important', 'will need', 'good practice', questions for audit committees; the NAO's are commitments in its own strategy ('We will'). No consequence for not meeting any of these is stated.
themes.checks: Only UK010 mentions a check, and it is on staff knowledge, not on the tool: 'testing of internal knowledge'. Trigger, comparator, metric, who and what happens with the result: not stated. Otherwise n/a.

themes.theme: Training for those who use AI tools and act on their outputs
themes.definition: Training, guidance and awareness aimed at the people who operate an AI tool or rely on its outputs, so that they understand its limits, spot errors and know their responsibilities.
themes.what_is_set_out: This is the part of the training material that bears most directly on checking outputs. UK174 says users and developers must be trained that 'the results from AI models can be false or biased', that users should be trained 'not to uncritically trust the outputs of generative AI or to rely exclusively on their responses', and that users must be educated on what data they may enter into public AI services. UK268 calls training 'essential, especially on the uncertainty of probabilistic systems, possible hallucinations of LLMs, and appropriate quality assurance measures' and expects guidance and training on a system's intended use and limitations in production. UK010 adds educating users in 'identifying errors and mitigations', training operators and overseers to recognise when a system is 'entering maloperation, and how to intervene', and training agents to spot unfair treatment of consumers. UK071 is the only document that checks whether such training works: briefings or training 'to see if users can correctly interpret and act on AI decisions'. UK136 states that operational staff 'must have enough knowledge of or training on the AI system to understand how to use it and act on its outputs' and makes training and explanations for non-specialists part of the supplier requirement; the NAO commits to skills 'for critically reviewing AI-assisted outputs'. DWP's policy (UK190) is the only document whose 'must' sits in a departmental policy: line managers must make employees, and contract managers suppliers, aware of their responsibilities; EHRC (UK216) asks public bodies to 'train staff and make sure they understand their responsibilities'. The ATRS template (UK087) asks bodies to record 'The required training those using the algorithmic tool must undertake, if applicable', which discloses training but does not require it. No document sets the content, length or pass standard of such training.
themes.holders: 'You' / the deploying organisation (UK174); the organisation, or not stated (UK268, UK010); the testing team, not stated (UK071); central government departments and operational or service staff (UK136); the NAO (NAO_AI_Strategy); DWP line managers and contract managers (UK190); public bodies in England (UK216); those using the algorithmic tool (UK087).
themes.binding: UK190: 'must' in a departmental policy, no consequence stated. UK174 and UK136: 'must' and 'need to' in non-statutory guidance. Others: 'should', 'essential', 'expected control', 'good practice', 'consideration'. UK268 names the risk if not met: insufficient training or guidance for end-users 'leading to misuse or misund[erstanding]', and 'Misuse or unintended use'. No sanction is stated anywhere.

(2) UK010 operators and overseers: trigger: during operation, when the system is 'entering maloperation'; compared against: not stated; metric: not stated; who: trained operators and overseers; result: they intervene.

themes.theme: Human reviewers and expert backstops for AI outputs
themes.definition: The people, and the tooling around them, who look at AI outputs before or after they are relied on, and the cases that are sent to them.
themes.what_is_set_out: Only a handful of passages say who actually reviews outputs. AI_Insights (large language model bias chapter) is the only passage that says which cases are sent to a human: 'Human review queues provide a final check for uncertain cases where automated systems cannot make confident decisions', and such cases 'can be routed to trained reviewers for human judgment'; who trains or supplies the reviewers is not stated. Another AI_Insights chapter (records management) says experts working in the relevant policy or business area 'can provide additional human assurance', and that tooling can record which reviewer is assigned which folders and record review decisions. UK071 treats staff as 'safety backstops (e.g. validating AI outputs)' whose skills can erode, so organisations should assess that risk. The NAO commits to developing its staff's 'skills for critically reviewing AI-assisted outputs'. None of these passages sets the confidence threshold for routing, the share of outputs to be reviewed, the reviewers' workload, or what reviewers compare outputs against.
themes.holders: Trained reviewers, with the operator of the application not stated (AI_Insights, LLM bias); experts working in the policy or business area (AI_Insights, records management); organisations (UK071); the NAO for its own staff.
themes.binding: Permissive: 'can', 'can provide', 'Tooling can help'; UK071 'should' assess skill loss; the NAO's is a commitment. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: uncertainty, i.e. 'uncertain cases where automated systems cannot make confident decisions' (AI_Insights); otherwise not stated. Compared against: human judgment; no reference standard is stated. Metric or threshold: not stated (no confidence cut-off is given). Who: trained reviewers; policy or business experts; staff acting as backstops. What happens with the result: in the records-management use, review stages and decisions are recorded in tooling; otherwise not stated.

themes.definition: Software, benchmarks, methods and expertise named as means to test an AI tool's performance, fairness, explainability or security, or to check AI-generated output.
themes.what_is_set_out: Most passages name tools without providing them. The only government-released software named for evaluating model outputs is Inspect, 'an open-source model evaluation framework released by the UK AI Safety Institute', which UK071 says teams 'should also consider' for LLMs; UK071 otherwise recommends automated test harnesses, testing built into CI/CD pipelines, and SHAP or LIME combined with domain expert review and user comprehension checks, but states that it 'does not mandate specific tools' and leaves the choice to departments. UK174 notes that ML hosting platforms 'often include evaluation tools' (Vertex AI, Prompt Flow). AI_Insights lists fairness toolkits from IBM, Microsoft, Google, the University of Chicago and PyMetrics, RAG retrieval benchmarks that 'provide standardised datasets', HuggingFace training frameworks, developer forums as a source of error reports, and third-party static analysis tools that 'should be used' to complement AI coding assistants, which is in effect a check on AI-written code; it also points to its own LLM Testing and Evaluation Metrics insights, whose content is not in the coded set. UK099 asks teams to consult technical experts and research when choosing explainability methods, and UK086 points to Service Manual guidance on setting performance metrics. UK082 recommends building 'government-backed high-quality assurance tools that assess whether AI systems perform as claimed and work as intended', a proposal rather than an existing tool. No passage gives a metric, a threshold, a reference dataset for the public body's own task, or a rule for re-testing after a change of model version or prompt.
themes.holders: Teams and departments (UK071); 'you' (UK174, UK099); mostly not stated (AI_Insights); providers named: UK AI Safety Institute, Google, Microsoft, IBM, University of Chicago, PyMetrics, HuggingFace, benchmark creators, Snyk, Aikido; government (UK082, as a recommendation).
themes.binding: Mostly mentions. UK071 'should also consider' Inspect and departments 'should select tools', while stating it mandates none; AI_Insights says static analysis tools 'should be used'; UK082 is a recommendation whose acceptance is not recorded. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: continuous, through CI/CD pipelines (UK071); at evaluation of RAG systems (AI_Insights); otherwise not stated. Compared against: standardised benchmark datasets (AI_Insights, RAG); the system's claimed performance and intended function (UK082, proposal); the features that influenced a sample output (SHAP/LIME, UK071); otherwise not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated (UK086 only points to guidance on setting performance metrics). Who: teams and departments, sometimes using providers' platforms. What happens with the result: not stated.

themes.theme: Resources for impact evaluation of AI interventions
themes.definition: Guidance, expert support, data and planning resources for evaluating what an AI intervention actually achieves, drawn mainly from the evaluation guidance in UK133.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK133 says it 'complements, and should be read in conjunction with, the Magenta Book', asks that appropriate resources for evaluation be set out 'at the delivery planning stage', points to 'Evaluation colleagues' who 'can support in identifying proportionate approaches', and to outside guidance on randomised controlled trials, sample sizes and rapid evaluation (Behavioural Insights Team, Office for Health Improvement and Disparities). Evaluators 'should work with relevant stakeholders' to find data already collected that could serve as a baseline. UK133 also notes that preliminary evidence may come from 'assurance activities conducted to assess the functioning and safety of the AI tool', such as red teaming, which links tool-level testing to outcome evaluation. Four hypothetical case studies (grant-fraud flagging, LLM briefing summaries, a citizen chatbot, NHS support) illustrate challenges but are not stated to be followed. UK174 adds that user researchers should be involved from the start so that 'research and evaluation is designed into' the solution. The resources are guidance and people within government; no money or time allowance for evaluation is stated.
themes.holders: Those designing or delivering an AI intervention (nearest named actor; the holder of 'set out appropriate resources' is not stated); evaluators; evaluation colleagues; HM Treasury (Magenta Book) and its Evaluation Task Force; Behavioural Insights Team and OHID as outside sources; project teams and user researchers (UK174).
themes.binding: Non-statutory: 'should be read in conjunction with', 'it is important', 'should'; other resources are pointed to. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: planned at the delivery planning stage, with a baseline established before the intervention.
